cards.title: Keyboard differences between Windows and Macs

depth.text: someone mapped out why **Windows and Mac keyboards** **differ on names, shortcuts, and key behavior**

Windows calls one key **Backspace**, while Mac calls it **Delete**; Windows’s Delete is Mac’s **Forward Delete**. On Macs, pressing Option with keys that type characters can produce extra characters; on many non-US keyboards, AltGr does something similar.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise Mac’s Command shortcuts as more ergonomic and logical; others say the platform’s key conventions are confusing enough to make switching difficult.

cards.title: A Terminal Protocol for Program Status (OSC 7501)

depth.text: someone wrote a **terminal protocol** that lets programs say when they're **working**, waiting, finished, or failed

The spec uses **OSC 7501**: programs send states like idle, working, blocked, done, or error through the terminal's existing **pty**. Optional fields can name the app and carry a message, while **hierarchical IDs** let programs report multiple tasks. The author says he made proof-of-concept integrations in Terraform, Claude Code, Codex, and Homebrew, each no more than a dozen lines.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters would rather extend OSC 3008 or stick with terminal bells; others welcome a dedicated protocol, especially for spotting when programs need input.

comments.text: This is important (and TIL OSC 3008, how do we all keep up?!), but I want something adjacent to this... perhaps people can point me in a direction. This OSC 7501 pushes state from Program to Terminal; with an explicit running/idle/fubar "state" field but also K/V data. Then Terminal can provide interactions thereof, such as display it. What I want is for the Program to push the terminal some map…

The problem `OSC 7501` addresses would slot almost perfectly into [UAPI.15 OSC 3008]( https://uapi-group.org/specifications/specs/osc_context/#met... ). It's already implemented by `systemd` and is available in Ubuntu 26.04. I'd rather see `OSC 3008` being extended.

The BSDs have had a version of this for many, many years. If you hit ^T on the terminal, you deliver a SIGINFO to the application you're waiting for. By default, you get the program name, what its blocked on, and info about real/user/sys time and memory use. Starting an emacs window in the fg: % emacs
^T
load: 0.32 cmd: emacs-31.1 64938 [select] 2.89r 0.75u 0.06s 6% 122404k

Cool to see this, I've been toying around with custom notification OSCs through zellij and ghostty. Totally going to extend this for myself with a custom key that encodes a reverse route on each hop so I can easily jump to the window/tab/pane that emitted it, or send back custom actions into a given pane like a permission approve/deny.
The spec’s at https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status

cards.title: ADHD as a circadian rhythm disorder: evidence and implications for chronotherapy (2025)

depth.text: the article links **body-clock shifts** with ADHD and says **changing sleep habits** may ease symptoms

The authors describe **delayed sleep timing** and shifted biological markers in a substantial subgroup, but not everyone. A child sleep program improved symptoms and functioning; the authors propose **routine sleep screening**, fixed wake times and morning bright light, with selective melatonin—not reclassifying ADHD exclusively as a circadian disorder.
data: ADHD patients with delayed sleep/wake cycle

cards.camps: Two camps: some see a strong, actionable sleep link; others say correlation doesn't make ADHD a circadian disorder, with early-riser counterexamples.

What's the advantage of this approach vs cycle-accurate emulation? (I'd guess it can go faster, due to compiler optimization?) > The result is…

The days I gave up with demoscene. When PC killed Atari ST and Amiga scene (sorry to put you after amiguys, but life was always easier for you ;) ), all the magic of fixed hardware without tons of Mhz and RAM, when we were running after that cathode ray which wouldn't wait, exploiting hardware bugs to break those damn borders above, below and sideways, spending hours turning my head upside-down…

Wow, this brings back memories! I got my first PC (a 486 DX2-66) in 1994 and got a Creative Soundblaster graphics card + speakers later that year. Second reality was the first demo I had on that PC. I remember being blown away by the graphics and audio... I showed it off to everyone. Of course it looks quite quaint now, but at the time I had just upgraded from a Commodore 64!

this is mind boggling! although during the 90s might have started to shift to use C in damascene production, but when I was most active (90-94) we were hand rolling a lot of code in assembly. memory "management" was pretty basic at best, code and data occasionally separated. maybe for demos it was less of thing, but for smaller intros, writing into the code during runtime was maybe not everyday…

cards.title: Show HN: Making a flexible "neon" t-shirt with LED filaments

depth.text: someone is making a flexible **neon T-shirt** with **LED filaments**
One commenter asks whether **LED filament** is the same as EL wire; another describes a costume filament that shocked them, then measured **240V** despite the two AA batteries.

comments.text: Yeah I do kinda the same but I embed them into latex prosthetics. Like horns or protrusions for the face that you glue on. They're really good for a cyberpunkey vibe. I'm just casting some at the moment actually because we're coming up on Halloween soon. They look great but they're difficult to solder. Too little heat and it doesn't attach, too much and it damages them. The strip has some…
Looks solid, best of luck with it.
Author here, happy to answer any questions!

One of my kids had something like this built into a Halloween costume that their mom procured from Amazon. One of the filaments was blinking out within a day so I started running the length of the filament to figure out where the bad connection was. Unexpectedly it shocked the hell out of me. I put a meter on it and it was 240V. I couldn't believe I got such a nasty poke from 2 AA batteries.
That's a nice wearable!
